criticalCaveat: Distances along roads mapped in OpenStreetMap on 2015-04-24 — not travel times, not journeys, not hospital capacity. The damaged network applies every blockage observed between 26 April and early May as if all were present at once. Hospitals are those in the 2010 government list unless stated.

methodology.name: Observed blockages attached to the full 2015 road network
methodology.question: How many observed blockages sit on a road OpenStreetMap had mapped by April 2015, once minor roads and tracks are included?

inputs.role: every motorable road and health facility mapped by 2015-04-24
observed blocked roads and bridges out

methodology.spatialCoverage: The access envelope 83.8, 27, 86.8, 28.8 — central Nepal from Gorkha to Dolakha — on roads mapped in OpenStreetMap by 2015-04-24.
methodology.method: The Stage 5 matcher, unchanged, run against the all-class network: each marker attaches to its nearest edge, reported across tolerances, with the tolerance taken from the knee of the curve and capped at 100 m.
methodology.formula: d(marker, edge) = min segment-to-segment distance in UTM 45N
methodology.parameterJustification: The same knee rule and ceiling Stage 5 used, so the two results differ only in the network.
methodology.visualisation: Blockage markers on the map, matched ones joined to the road they cut.
methodology.validation: 54 of 184 markers attach at 25 m, against 21 on the Stage 5 major-road network.
limitations: A matched marker disables its whole junction-to-junction edge: right for connectivity, an over-statement for length.
A marker that matches nothing sat on a road not mapped in April 2015; it is counted, not dropped.

methodology.name: Distance to the nearest hospital, before and after the observed road damage
methodology.question: How far along mapped roads was the nearest hospital for the people in each 1 km cell, and how did the observed blockages change that?

inputs.role: every motorable road and health facility mapped by 2015-04-24
government health facility list (2010 vintage): the hospitals searched for
observed blocked roads and bridges out

methodology.spatialCoverage: The access envelope 83.8, 27, 86.8, 28.8 — central Nepal from Gorkha to Dolakha — on roads mapped in OpenStreetMap by 2015-04-24.
methodology.method: One multi-source Dijkstra outward from every hospital in the 2010 list at once, over the undirected road graph, with and without the matched blockages; each populated cell joins at its nearest junction within the snap limit, adding that straight-line leg. People are counted, not cells.
methodology.formula: access(cell) = snap(cell) + min over hospitals h of [ network(junction(cell), junction(h)) + snap(h) ]
methodology.parameterJustification: A 1 km cell centre lies up to 710 m from its edge, so 2 km covers the cell and a walk to the road; beyond it the cell is reported as having no mapped road nearby. One kilometre separates a real change from snapping noise. Both are re-run at other values and the table is published.
outputs: the same for the OpenStreetMap hospitals and for any clinical facility
methodology.visualisation: Populated cells coloured by change category; the example route traced before and after.
methodology.validation: 7941981 people within 2 km of a mapped road; median 7.45 km before and 7.45 km after; removing edges never shortened any distance.
limitations: Distance, not time: no road speeds exist for the date.
Every observed blockage is applied at once, although they were observed on different days and some cleared quickly.
The hospital list is from 2010. A hospital opened by 2015 is missing; one closed is still counted.
A nearer hospital is not a better one. No capacity, damage-to-hospital or service information is used, because none is available.

methodology.name: Rescue-access pressure by district: a Pareto set and its weighting sensitivity
methodology.question: Which districts combined the most people in strong shaking, the longest hospital distances and the most disrupted access — and how much does any ordering of them depend on the weights?

inputs.role: every motorable road and health facility mapped by 2015-04-24
government health facility list (2010 vintage): the hospitals searched for
observed blocked roads and bridges out

methodology.spatialCoverage: The access envelope 83.8, 27, 86.8, 28.8 — central Nepal from Gorkha to Dolakha — on roads mapped in OpenStreetMap by 2015-04-24. Districts with less than 90 per cent of their people inside the envelope are excluded, and listed.
methodology.method: Three measured criteria per district. The Pareto set (no other district is at least as high on all three and higher on one) needs no weights. Four weighting schemes are then applied to min-max normalised criteria and the resulting ranks compared.
methodology.formula: score_s(d) = sum_k w_sk * (x_dk - min_k) / (max_k - min_k), ranked per scheme s
methodology.parameterJustification: No weighting is defensible on its own, so none is chosen: four are run and the rank spread is the result.
outputs: districts in the top five under every scheme
methodology.visualisation: Districts outlined on the map, the Pareto set marked, with a small rank-spread chart.
methodology.validation: Pareto set: Chitawan, Dhading, Gorkha, Kathmandu, Nuwakot, Sindhuli, Sindhupalchok. In the top 5 under every scheme: Ramechhap, Sindhuli.
limitations: NOT A PRIORITY LIST and not a record of where help went. It compares measured conditions.
Each criterion inherits its own caveats: modelled shaking, 2010 hospitals, April-2015 roads.
Min-max normalisation is sensitive to the extreme district; the Pareto set is not.

methodology.name: Two example routes to hospital, before and after
methodology.question: For the most populous cell whose route lengthened, and the most populous cell whose route was cut, what did the route look like before and after the observed blockages?

inputs.role: every motorable road and health facility mapped by 2015-04-24
government health facility list (2010 vintage): the hospitals searched for
observed blocked roads and bridges out

methodology.spatialCoverage: Two 1 km cells, chosen by a stated rule; plus a before-and-after table for every UNOSAT analysis area with at least 20 sites.
methodology.method: The predecessor chain of each search, traced from the area’s junction back to its nearest hospital and drawn from the edge geometry.
methodology.visualisation: The two routes traced in turn, the cut marked where the first one fails.
methodology.validation: Detour example (Okhaldhunga): 8.8 km before, 14 km after. Cut example (Sindhuli): 49.13 km before, no mapped route after. Both routes end on the junction of the hospital their search reports.
limitations: An illustration of the method on one case, chosen by rule; not evidence of any journey that took place.
The destination is the nearest hospital in the 2010 list, not necessarily the one anyone used.

methodology.name: Do the 2010 government list and the April 2015 OpenStreetMap map agree on hospitals?
methodology.question: How many hospitals in each list have a counterpart in the other, and how far apart are they?

inputs.role: every motorable road and health facility mapped by 2015-04-24
government health facility list (2010 vintage): the hospitals searched for

methodology.spatialCoverage: The access envelope 83.8, 27, 86.8, 28.8 — central Nepal from Gorkha to Dolakha — on roads mapped in OpenStreetMap by 2015-04-24.
methodology.method: Nearest-neighbour great-circle distance from every hospital in one list to the other, reported as a curve over distance bands.
outputs: share of each list within 0.5, 1, 2 and 5 km of the other
methodology.visualisation: Both lists on the map in different marks; the curve in the detail panel.
methodology.validation: 38 hospitals in the 2010 list and 343 tagged hospital in OpenStreetMap inside the envelope.
limitations: OpenStreetMap "hospital" often tags a clinic; the government list distinguishes types. Disagreement is partly definitional.
Position error in either list is unknown; a counterpart within 500 m may still be a different facility.

blockageMatching.note: Stage 5 matched 21 of 184 on the motorway-to-tertiary network. The fuller 2015 network, which includes the minor roads and tracks most blockages sat on, is what lets more of them attach.

pressure.warning: A comparison of measured conditions per district, not a record of where help was needed or went, and not a priority list. The Pareto set needs no weights; the weighted rankings exist only to show how much the order depends on them.

detour.selectionRule: Among the 1 km cells whose nearest-hospital route became longer or switched hospital when the observed blockages are applied, the most populous one whose detour is at least the population-weighted median detour. A typical case, chosen by the pipeline, not by hand.

cut.selectionRule: The most populous 1 km cell that had a mapped road route to a hospital before and none after the observed blockages are applied. Chosen by the pipeline, not by hand.
